overview: Data quality is the measure of how fit data is for its intended use, assessed across dimensions such as accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness.

Data quality engineering operationalizes these dimensions through automated checks, profiling, monitoring, anomaly detection, and data SLAs/SLOs so quality is continuously measured rather than assumed.
Frameworks like Great Expectations, dbt tests, Soda, and Deequ embed quality assertions directly into pipelines, failing or quarantining bad data before it reaches consumers.
learningObjectives: Define and measure the core data quality dimensions and translate them into concrete, automated checks.
Apply data quality frameworks, profiling, and anomaly detection to monitor pipelines and enforce data SLAs.
Design a quality strategy that quarantines or blocks bad data and surfaces issues through alerting and observability.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Data quality is the degree to which a dataset satisfies explicit and implicit requirements for its intended use, quantified along measurable dimensions (accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness, and others) and enforced via validation rules, statistical profiling, and continuous monitoring against defined thresholds and service-level objectives.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Data quality is about trusting your data. Just as a factory inspects parts for defects before they go into a product, a data team checks that values are correct, nothing important is missing, formats are valid, records are not duplicated, and the data arrives on time, so that dashboards and models built on it can be trusted.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Concerns about data quality date to the data warehousing and master-data-management era of the 1990s, with formal dimension frameworks like Richard Wang and Diane Strong's 1996 work on data quality dimensions. The modern shift came with the 'data observability' movement (Monte Carlo, ~2019) and the rise of pipeline-native testing tools (Great Expectations 2018, dbt tests, Soda, Amazon Deequ), moving quality from after-the-fact cleanup to continuous, automated enforcement.

whyItMatters.business: Bad data drives wrong decisions, broken dashboards, failed regulatory reports, and lost customer trust; high-quality data is the foundation of reliable analytics, ML, and compliance, directly protecting revenue and reputation.
whyItMatters.engineering: Automated quality checks catch upstream breakages (schema drift, null spikes, duplicate loads) before they propagate, turning silent data corruption into actionable, debuggable failures.
whyItMatters.scalability: As data volume and the number of sources grow, manual inspection is impossible; programmatic checks, profiling, and anomaly detection are the only way to maintain trust at scale.
whyItMatters.cost: Catching defects early is far cheaper than reprocessing downstream tables, retraining models on bad data, or remediating incorrect business decisions; data downtime has direct financial cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Data SLAs/SLOs make reliability of data products measurable and enforceable, the same way uptime SLOs do for services.

coreComponents.name: Quality Dimensions
coreComponents.definition: The measurable axes along which data quality is assessed: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, and uniqueness.
coreComponents.purpose: To give a structured, quantifiable vocabulary for what 'good' data means for a given use case.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Each dimension maps to concrete metrics and checks (e.g., completeness -> null rate, uniqueness -> duplicate count).
coreComponents.examples: Completeness: % of non-null email values; Validity: % of rows where email matches a regex.

coreComponents.name: Validation / Test Framework
coreComponents.definition: Tooling that expresses quality assertions as code and executes them against data in the pipeline.
coreComponents.purpose: To enforce expectations automatically and fail or quarantine data that violates them.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Run row- and table-level checks, produce pass/fail results, and gate downstream steps.
coreComponents.examples: Great Expectations expectation suites, dbt schema/data tests (not_null, unique, accepted_values), Soda checks, Amazon Deequ constraints.

coreComponents.name: Monitoring & Observability
coreComponents.definition: Continuous tracking of data health metrics, freshness, volume, schema, and distributions over time.
coreComponents.purpose: To detect anomalies, degradation, and SLA breaches and alert the right owners.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Collect metrics, baseline normal behavior, detect anomalies, and route alerts.
coreComponents.examples: Freshness/volume monitors, null-rate trend alerts, distribution-shift detection (data observability platforms).

internalWorking: During profiling, the system scans a dataset to compute statistics per column (null count, distinct count, min/max, mean, distribution, common patterns) that characterize 'normal' data.

Validation rules (derived from profiling or business requirements) are evaluated against incoming data: each check returns pass/fail plus a measured metric (e.g., null_rate = 0.3%), compared against a threshold.

Results feed monitoring: metrics are stored over time, anomaly detectors flag deviations from baselines (e.g., a sudden null spike or row-count drop), and failures trigger alerts, block promotion, or route bad records to a quarantine table while compliant data proceeds.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: Source -> Ingest -> Profile (baseline stats) -> Validate (rules/expectations) -> Pass: load to trusted layer | Fail: quarantine + alert -> Monitor metrics over time -> Anomaly detection / SLA tracking -> Dashboards & alerts
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. A daily orders batch lands in a staging table; a profiling step computes row count, null rates, and distinct counts per column.
2. Validation runs expectations: order_id is unique and not null, amount is non-negative, currency is in an accepted set, order_date is within the expected window (validity/consistency).
3. Completeness check finds email null rate jumped from 1% to 18% versus the historical baseline, breaching the threshold.
4. The pipeline quarantines failing rows, marks the batch as failed for the email metric, raises an alert to the data owner, and a freshness monitor confirms whether the batch met its arrival SLA.

keyTerminology.meaning: The degree to which data correctly reflects the real-world entity or event it represents.
keyTerminology.importance: Inaccurate data (wrong address, wrong amount) leads directly to wrong decisions; hardest dimension to verify without a source of truth.

keyTerminology.meaning: The extent to which all required data is present (no missing values or records).
keyTerminology.importance: Missing values skew aggregates and break joins; measured via null rates and expected-vs-actual record counts.

keyTerminology.meaning: The absence of contradictions for the same data across records, tables, or systems.
keyTerminology.importance: Inconsistent values (a customer with two different birthdates) undermine trust and reconciliation.

keyTerminology.meaning: Whether data is available when expected and reflects a sufficiently recent state (freshness + latency).
keyTerminology.importance: Stale data leads to decisions on outdated information; enforced via freshness SLAs.

keyTerminology.meaning: Whether data conforms to defined formats, types, ranges, and business rules.
keyTerminology.importance: Invalid values (malformed emails, out-of-range ages) break downstream parsing and logic.

keyTerminology.meaning: The absence of unwanted duplicate records or key collisions.
keyTerminology.importance: Duplicates inflate counts and revenue and corrupt joins; checked via primary-key/duplicate detection.

importantConcepts.explanation: A Data SLA is an agreement on data quality and delivery (e.g., 'orders table is fresh by 6 AM with <0.1% null order_ids 99.9% of days'). SLOs are the measurable targets and SLIs the indicators (freshness, null rate, volume) tracked against them, analogous to service reliability SLOs.

The exploratory analysis of a dataset to compute column-level statistics and patterns (nulls, cardinality, ranges, distributions, formats). Profiling both reveals quality issues and bootstraps expectations and anomaly baselines.
Statistical or ML-based detection of deviations from a learned baseline (row-count drops, null spikes, distribution shift, freshness lag). It catches unknown-unknowns that hand-written rules miss.

variationsAndTypes: **Schema/structural checks:** column existence, data types, schema-drift detection.
**Row-level / record checks:** not_null, range, regex/format validity, accepted-value sets on individual rows.
**Aggregate/table checks:** row counts, distinct counts, null rates, referential integrity, distribution metrics.
**Freshness/volume checks:** latest-timestamp recency and expected row-count ranges (timeliness).
**Cross-source reconciliation:** comparing counts/sums between source and target to detect drift or loss.
advantages: **Trustworthy analytics & ML:** Consumers can rely on data without manual re-verification.
**Early defect detection:** Catches upstream breakages before they propagate downstream.
**Measurable reliability:** Data SLAs/SLOs make data-product reliability explicit and enforceable.
**Faster debugging:** Failing checks pinpoint where and how data broke.
disadvantages: **Maintenance overhead:** Rules and expectations must evolve with the data; stale checks cause false alarms.
**Alert fatigue:** Too many or poorly tuned checks/anomaly alerts desensitize teams.
**Compute cost:** Profiling and full-table checks on large datasets consume resources.
**False sense of security:** Passing tests only proves the asserted expectations, not overall correctness.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Apply rigorous quality checks on high-value, widely consumed, or regulated data products (financial reporting, ML training data, customer-facing metrics), and at ingestion boundaries where external/untrusted data enters.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid heavyweight checks on every transient/intermediate table or for exploratory one-off analyses where the cost and maintenance of full validation outweigh the risk; sample or use lightweight checks instead.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Data quality is like quality control in a restaurant kitchen. Ingredients are inspected on delivery (validity, completeness), the chef tastes dishes before serving (accuracy), recipes are followed consistently across cooks (consistency), food is served fresh and on time (timeliness), and you do not plate the same order twice (uniqueness). A bad ingredient caught at delivery is cheap to reject; the same defect discovered by the customer is far costlier.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Data quality is a one-time cleanup project.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Data quality is a continuous discipline. Sources change, schemas drift, and volumes shift, so quality must be monitored continuously with automated checks, not fixed once and forgotten.

commonMisconceptions.myth: If the pipeline ran successfully, the data is good.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A pipeline can succeed technically while loading wrong, incomplete, stale, or duplicated data. Success of the job and quality of the data are independent and must be validated separately.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Run checks where the data lives (pushdown to the warehouse/engine), sample for expensive distribution checks, and partition checks by date so they scale with incremental loads rather than full scans.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Make checks deterministic and idempotent, version expectation suites alongside pipeline code, and ensure failed checks reliably block promotion or quarantine data rather than silently passing.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Quarantine (rather than drop) bad records so they can be inspected and reprocessed; ensure a failing check on one column does not lose the whole batch unnecessarily.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Track quality SLIs (freshness, null rate, volume, distinct counts, duplicate counts) over time with dashboards, baselines, and anomaly detection, not just instantaneous pass/fail.
productionConsiderations.security: Profiling and quarantine stores can expose PII; apply masking, access controls, and retention limits to quality artifacts and avoid logging sensitive failing values.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Schedule expensive checks on cadence rather than every micro-batch, use approximate/sampled metrics where exact counts are unnecessary, and prune redundant checks.
productionConsiderations.performance: Prefer set-based SQL checks and engine pushdown over row-by-row Python; index/partition columns used in checks; aggregate metrics in a single pass where possible.

codeExamples.title: dbt Schema & Data Tests for Core Dimensions
codeExamples.overview: Declaratively enforce uniqueness, completeness, validity, and consistency on a dbt model using built-in and expressed tests in a schema.yml file.
codeExamples.code:
version: 2

models:
  - name: orders
    description: "Cleaned orders fact table"
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: "Primary key"
        tests:
          - unique          # uniqueness dimension
          - not_null        # completeness dimension
      - name: customer_id
        tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:   # consistency / referential integrity
              to: ref('customers')
              field: customer_id
      - name: status
        tests:
          - accepted_values: # validity dimension
              values: ['placed', 'shipped', 'delivered', 'cancelled']
      - name: amount
        tests:
          - dbt_utils.accepted_range:  # validity (range)
              min_value: 0
codeExamples.breakdown: Each test maps to a dimension: `unique`/`not_null` cover uniqueness and completeness on the primary key; `relationships` enforces referential consistency to the customers model; `accepted_values` enforces validity of the status enum; `accepted_range` enforces a non-negative amount. Running `dbt test` executes them as SQL and fails the run on violations.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: `dbt test` reports PASS/FAIL per test; e.g., 'FAIL 3 when testing unique on order_id' if duplicate keys exist, blocking the model from being trusted.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Tests that always pass because the model already filtered bad rows; missing dbt_utils package install; treating warnings as errors (configure severity).
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Set `severity: warn` for non-blocking checks, use `store_failures: true` to persist failing rows for debugging, and limit relationship tests on huge tables to incremental partitions.

codeExamples.title: Great Expectations Suite (Python)
codeExamples.overview: Define and validate expectations across completeness, uniqueness, validity, and range using Great Expectations on a pandas dataframe.
codeExamples.code:
import great_expectations as gx
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_parquet("orders.parquet")
context = gx.get_context()
validator = context.sources.pandas_default.read_dataframe(df)

# Uniqueness
validator.expect_column_values_to_be_unique("order_id")
# Completeness
validator.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null("order_id")
validator.expect_column_values_to_not_be_null("customer_id", mostly=0.99)
# Validity (format + set)
validator.expect_column_values_to_match_regex("email", r"^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$")
validator.expect_column_values_to_be_in_set("status",
    ["placed", "shipped", "delivered", "cancelled"])
# Validity (range) + Timeliness
validator.expect_column_values_to_be_between("amount", min_value=0)
validator.expect_column_max_to_be_between("order_date",
    min_value="2020-01-01", max_value="2030-01-01")

results = validator.validate()
print("SUCCESS" if results.success else "FAILED")
codeExamples.breakdown: Each expectation targets a dimension: uniqueness (be_unique), completeness (not_null, with mostly=0.99 tolerating up to 1% nulls), validity (regex for email format, be_in_set for status, be_between for amount range), and a timeliness/sanity bound on order_date. validate() returns a success flag plus per-expectation results used to gate the pipeline.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A validation result object; prints 'SUCCESS' if all expectations pass or 'FAILED' with details (e.g., unexpected_count for email regex) when violations occur.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Over-strict expectations causing flapping failures; forgetting `mostly` tolerances; not persisting results to Data Docs for visibility.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Auto-generate an initial suite via profiling, use `mostly` to tolerate known noise, and run against the warehouse via SQL execution engine rather than pulling data into pandas for large tables.

codeExamples.title: SQL Data Quality Profiling & Checks
codeExamples.overview: A single SQL pass that profiles a table and computes metrics for completeness, uniqueness, validity, and freshness, comparable against thresholds.
codeExamples.code:
SELECT
  COUNT(*)                                            AS row_count,
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(order_id)                           AS null_order_ids,        -- completeness
  COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)                  AS duplicate_order_ids,   -- uniqueness
  AVG(CASE WHEN amount < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)          AS pct_negative_amount,   -- validity
  AVG(CASE WHEN email NOT LIKE '%@%.%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS pct_invalid_email,  -- validity
  MAX(order_date)                                      AS latest_order,          -- timeliness
  DATEDIFF('hour', MAX(order_date), CURRENT_TIMESTAMP) AS hours_since_latest      -- freshness/timeliness
FROM staging.orders
WHERE order_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '1 day';
codeExamples.breakdown: One scan computes multiple dimension metrics: null_order_ids (completeness) and duplicate_order_ids (uniqueness) compare COUNT vs COUNT(DISTINCT); pct_negative_amount and pct_invalid_email (validity) use conditional averages; latest_order and hours_since_latest measure freshness (timeliness). A wrapper job compares each metric to a threshold and fails/alerts on breach.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: A single row of metrics, e.g., row_count=120345, null_order_ids=0, duplicate_order_ids=12, pct_negative_amount=0.0, pct_invalid_email=0.004, hours_since_latest=2 — duplicates here would trip the uniqueness check.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Full-table scans on huge tables (filter by partition/date); LIKE-based validity being too loose; ignoring timezone in freshness comparisons.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Filter by partition to scale incrementally, push the query down to the warehouse, and store the metric row in a history table to enable trend-based anomaly detection.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A subscription business reports daily revenue and active-user metrics to executives and feeds a churn model. Occasional upstream issues (duplicate loads, null user_ids, stale data, malformed currency codes) silently corrupted dashboards and model inputs, eroding trust. The goal is automated data quality enforcement with SLAs so bad data is caught and quarantined before it reaches consumers.
endToEndExample.inputData: Daily events and transactions from app and billing systems, landing in a staging schema; each transaction has transaction_id, user_id, amount, currency, and event_timestamp.
endToEndExample.architecture: Ingestion to staging, then a dbt + Great Expectations quality gate, then load to a trusted analytics layer. A quarantine table holds failing rows. A metrics-history table feeds an anomaly-detection job and a data-observability dashboard; alerts route to the owning team. SLAs are defined per table (freshness by 6 AM, null transaction_id < 0.01%, duplicate rate = 0).
processingSteps: 1. Profiling computes per-column stats on the staging batch (row count, null rates, distinct counts, currency value distribution) and writes them to a metrics-history table.

2. Validation runs dimension checks: uniqueness (transaction_id), completeness (user_id, amount not null), validity (currency in ISO set, amount >= 0), timeliness (latest event within freshness SLA), and consistency (user_id exists in users dimension).
3. Rows failing row-level checks are routed to a quarantine table with the failed-rule annotation; the remainder proceed.
4. Aggregate/table checks and anomaly detection compare today's metrics to the rolling baseline (e.g., row-count drop > 30%, null spike) and gate promotion to the trusted layer.
5. On any SLA breach, an alert fires to the data owner with the failing metric and a link to the failing rows; passing data is published and dashboards refresh.
endToEndExample.output: A trusted analytics layer with deduplicated, complete, valid, fresh transactions; a quarantine table of rejected rows for triage; and a quality dashboard tracking each dimension's SLI against its SLA over time.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Dashboards show freshness lag, null rates, duplicate counts, row-count trends, and distribution shifts per table; anomaly detection baselines normal ranges; SLA compliance is tracked as a percentage over rolling windows.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Row-level failures quarantine the offending rows; table-level/anomaly failures block promotion and alert; freshness breaches alert immediately. Quarantined rows are inspected and either fixed-and-reprocessed or confirmed as genuinely bad.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Executive dashboards and the churn model now consume only validated data; silent corruption incidents dropped sharply, mean-time-to-detection fell from days to minutes via anomaly alerts, and data SLAs gave consumers measurable confidence in the data products.

industryUseCases.problem: Thousands of derived datasets had unclear, inconsistent quality, making it hard for analysts to know which tables to trust.
industryUseCases.solution: Airbnb built data quality scoring and certification (e.g., the Midas/Dataportal effort) with standardized checks, ownership, and trust signals on datasets.
industryUseCases.benefits: Consumers can identify certified, high-quality datasets, reducing duplicated and untrustworthy data and improving decision reliability across the company.

industryUseCases.problem: Teams discovered data incidents (freshness, volume, schema, distribution issues) only after stakeholders complained, causing 'data downtime'.
industryUseCases.solution: Automated data observability that monitors freshness, volume, schema, and distribution, learns baselines, and detects anomalies across the warehouse.
industryUseCases.benefits: Incidents are detected automatically with lineage-aware root-cause analysis, cutting time-to-detection and time-to-resolution and reducing data downtime.

industryUseCases.problem: Validating data quality on very large datasets in Spark required efficient, declarative, automatable checks.
industryUseCases.solution: Amazon developed Deequ, a library for defining 'unit tests for data' (completeness, uniqueness, constraints) and metric computation/anomaly detection on Spark.
industryUseCases.benefits: Scalable, declarative quality verification embedded in big-data pipelines, catching constraint violations before bad data is consumed by downstream services and ML.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Push checks down to the warehouse/Spark engine to compute metrics in-place, filter by partition for incremental loads, and use approximate algorithms (HyperLogLog for distinct counts) where exactness is unnecessary so checks scale with data growth.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Quarantine bad records instead of dropping them, make quality jobs idempotent so reruns are safe, and ensure a check failure produces a clear, recoverable state (failed batch with reason) rather than a silent partial load.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Run quality gates as part of the orchestrated pipeline with retries and clear ownership; keep metrics-history and quarantine stores on durable, replicated storage so quality state survives node failures.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Versioned expectation suites and metrics history allow reconstruction of what 'good' looked like; quarantined and source data enable safe reprocessing after recovery without losing failed records.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Combine multiple column metrics into a single SQL pass, prefer set-based checks over row-by-row Python, cache profiling baselines, and schedule expensive distribution checks less frequently than cheap freshness/volume checks.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Tier checks by data value (rigorous on critical tables, lightweight on intermediates), sample for expensive checks, and prune redundant or always-passing rules to cut compute spend.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Treat quarantine tables, profiling outputs, and failure logs as potentially containing PII; apply masking, least-privilege access, and retention limits, and avoid emitting sensitive failing values into alerts.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Track the five pillars of data observability (freshness, volume, schema, distribution, lineage) with baselines and anomaly detection; expose per-dimension SLIs and SLA compliance on dashboards and alert on breaches, not on every passing run.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Map every dimension to an explicit check, validate at ingestion boundaries and before publication, reconcile counts/sums across source and target, and store results historically to enable trend analysis and anomaly detection.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log per-check metric and pass/fail with batch and table context; route alerts to dataset owners with the failing rule, measured value, threshold, and a link to quarantined rows; suppress duplicate/noisy alerts and escalate only sustained or SLA-breaching failures.

recommendedPractices: **Map each quality dimension to concrete, automated checks** (e.g., completeness -> null-rate thresholds, uniqueness -> duplicate counts).
**Validate at boundaries**: check data on ingestion (untrusted input) and before publishing to consumers.
**Define data SLAs/SLOs** for critical tables (freshness, null rate, volume) and track SLI compliance over time.
**Quarantine, don't drop**, failing records so they can be inspected and reprocessed.
**Use profiling to bootstrap expectations** and feed anomaly-detection baselines rather than guessing thresholds.
engineeringStandards: Quality checks live in version control alongside pipeline/transformation code and are run in CI and in production.
Every critical dataset has a named owner and a documented SLA.
Failing checks must gate promotion (block or quarantine), not merely warn, for critical data products.
designRecommendations: Tier checks by data value: rigorous on critical/published tables, lightweight on transient intermediates.
Combine cheap fast checks (freshness, volume, nulls) run frequently with expensive checks (distribution, reconciliation) run on a cadence.
Prefer engine pushdown / set-based SQL over row-by-row processing for scalability.
namingConventions: Name checks by table + dimension + column, e.g., `orders__completeness__order_id_not_null`.
Name quarantine tables consistently, e.g., `orders_quarantine` or `<table>_dq_failures`.
documentationStandards: Document each table's SLA (freshness, completeness, uniqueness targets) and owner.
Document what each check asserts, its threshold, and severity (warn vs error).
Maintain a data catalog/Data Docs with trust/certification signals visible to consumers.
testingStrategies: Run quality tests in CI against sample/staging data so schema or logic changes that break expectations are caught pre-deploy.
Use fault injection (inject nulls, duplicates, stale timestamps) to verify checks actually fail when they should.
Backtest anomaly-detection thresholds against historical incidents to tune sensitivity and reduce false positives.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a successful pipeline run as proof of good data.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Teams monitor job success/failure but not the content of the data itself.
commonMistakes.impact: Wrong, incomplete, stale, or duplicated data flows to dashboards and models undetected until stakeholders complain.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Add explicit data quality checks (dimensions) that validate the data content and gate publication independently of job success.

commonMistakes.mistake: Setting checks without baselines, causing alert fatigue or missed issues.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Thresholds are guessed rather than derived from profiling/history.
commonMistakes.impact: Too-strict checks flap and get ignored; too-loose checks miss real problems; either way trust in alerts erodes.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Profile the data to establish baselines, use tolerances (e.g., mostly), and use anomaly detection on historical metrics for dynamic thresholds.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping or silently filtering bad records.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Pipelines are written to 'just keep going' by discarding rows that fail checks.
commonMistakes.impact: Silent data loss, skewed aggregates, and no audit trail of what was rejected or why.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Quarantine failing rows to a dedicated table with the failed-rule annotation, alert owners, and reprocess after fixing.

comparisonSection.optionA: Pipeline-native testing (Great Expectations / dbt tests / Soda)
comparisonSection.explanation: Pipeline-native testing asserts known, explicit rules inline and can block bad data before it lands. Observability passively monitors freshness/volume/schema/distribution and detects unknown anomalies after the fact. They are complementary: tests for known expectations, observability for unknown-unknowns.

Quarantining preserves bad records with annotations for triage and reprocessing and keeps an audit trail. Dropping loses data silently, skews metrics, and provides no way to diagnose or recover, which is almost always the wrong default.

Static thresholds are simple and predictable but brittle as data evolves. Anomaly detection adapts to seasonality and trends and catches novel issues, at the cost of complexity and tuning. Mature setups combine hard static rules for must-not-violate constraints with anomaly detection for drift.

beginnerQuestions.question: What are the main dimensions of data quality?
beginnerQuestions.answer: The core dimensions are accuracy (matches reality), completeness (no missing values/records), consistency (no contradictions across systems), timeliness (fresh and on time), validity (conforms to formats/ranges/rules), and uniqueness (no unwanted duplicates).
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Name all six and give a one-line example check per dimension; interviewers want to see you can operationalize each, not just list them.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between validity and accuracy?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Validity means data conforms to a defined format/rule (e.g., an email matches the email regex, age is 0-120). Accuracy means the value is actually correct in the real world (the email is the person's real email). A value can be valid but inaccurate.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: The classic example: a well-formatted but wrong phone number is valid but not accurate. Accuracy usually needs a source of truth to verify.

intermediateQuestions.question: How would you implement data quality checks in a pipeline, and which tools would you use?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Map each dimension to checks and run them as a gate in the pipeline: not_null/null-rate (completeness), unique/duplicate counts (uniqueness), regex/accepted_values/range (validity), relationships (consistency), and freshness/volume (timeliness). Tools include dbt tests, Great Expectations, Soda, and Amazon Deequ, with results gating promotion or quarantining bad rows.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: A strong answer ties dimensions to concrete checks and names where in the pipeline they run (ingestion boundary, pre-publication) plus the quarantine pattern.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is a data SLA and how does it differ from data profiling?
intermediateQuestions.answer: A data SLA is an agreement on a data product's quality and delivery (e.g., fresh by 6 AM, null order_id < 0.01%, zero duplicates), with SLOs as targets and SLIs as the tracked indicators. Profiling is the exploratory computation of column statistics (nulls, cardinality, ranges, distributions) used to understand data and set realistic SLA thresholds and baselines.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Distinguish the commitment (SLA) from the analysis (profiling); profiling informs the thresholds an SLA promises.

advancedQuestions.question: How do pipeline tests and data observability differ, and why use both?
advancedQuestions.answer: Pipeline tests (dbt/Great Expectations) assert explicit, known expectations inline and can block bad data before it lands; they cover known-knowns. Data observability passively monitors freshness, volume, schema, and distribution, learns baselines, and detects anomalies (unknown-unknowns) often after the data lands. Mature stacks combine inline tests for known constraints with observability for drift and novel incidents.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Mention the five observability pillars and that tests fail-closed while observability is detective; together they cover both known and unknown failure modes.

advancedQuestions.question: How would you detect anomalies in data quality metrics at scale?
advancedQuestions.answer: Persist metric history (row counts, null rates, distinct counts, freshness lag) per partition, establish baselines accounting for seasonality, and apply statistical methods (z-score/IQR, time-series models, or ML detectors) to flag deviations like volume drops, null spikes, or distribution shift. Combine hard static rules for must-not-violate constraints with adaptive detection for drift, and tune thresholds via backtesting to control false positives.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Emphasize storing metrics over time, seasonality, and the tradeoff between sensitivity and alert fatigue.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Stakeholders report that yesterday's revenue dashboard was double the real figure. How do you diagnose and prevent recurrence?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Double revenue strongly suggests a uniqueness/duplicate-load issue. Diagnose by checking COUNT vs COUNT(DISTINCT) on the key and comparing row counts to baseline; then add preventive checks and idempotent loads.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Confirm duplicates via duplicate_order_ids = COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT transaction_id) and a row-count spike versus baseline (likely a double-run load). Fix by making the load idempotent (MERGE/upsert or delete-insert by partition), add a uniqueness check on transaction_id and a volume anomaly check that gates publication, and quarantine duplicates. Add monitoring so a future duplicate load alerts before reaching the dashboard.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design a data quality framework for a company with hundreds of tables feeding analytics and ML, where consumers don't know which data to trust.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: A layered framework: ingestion-boundary validation for untrusted sources; pipeline-native tests (dbt/GE) mapping each dimension to checks; a metrics-history store feeding anomaly detection; a quarantine pattern for bad records; per-table SLAs with named owners; and a catalog with trust/certification signals so consumers see quality. Observability monitors freshness/volume/schema/distribution across all tables.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: More checks improve trust but add maintenance and compute cost and risk alert fatigue; tier rigor by data value. Static rules are simple but brittle; anomaly detection adapts but needs tuning. Blocking guarantees quality but can stall pipelines; quarantine balances throughput and safety.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Push checks down to the warehouse/Spark, partition checks for incremental loads, use approximate metrics where exact is unneeded, run cheap checks frequently and expensive ones on cadence, and centralize ownership and alerting so the framework scales to hundreds of tables without per-table bespoke code.

keyTakeaways: Data quality is measured across six core dimensions (accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity, uniqueness), each of which should map to concrete automated checks.
Quality is a continuous discipline, not a one-time cleanup; enforce it with pipeline-native tests (dbt, Great Expectations, Soda, Deequ) plus profiling, monitoring, and anomaly detection.
Data SLAs/SLOs make data-product reliability measurable and enforceable (freshness, null rate, volume), analogous to service uptime SLOs.
Validate data at boundaries and before publication, quarantine failing records instead of dropping them, and alert dataset owners on SLA breaches.
Combine explicit tests (known-knowns) with data observability and anomaly detection (unknown-unknowns), tiering rigor by data value to balance trust, cost, and alert fatigue.
